teaching_cases.assumptions: Original fictional example. Draft claim: "The town should try opening the library on Sundays." Worked analysis against three criteria. Who acts: "the town" is vague — no office or council named that could actually decide or fund a pilot; the actor fails. What exactly to do: "try opening" names a direction, not a step — no hours, staffing, or duration; the action fails. What counts as success: no measure is stated, so any result could be declared a success or failure; the success test fails. Revised version that passes all three: "The town council should run a six-week Sunday-opening pilot at the main branch, 12 to 5, with two staff on duty, and continue only if average Sunday visits cover the added staffing cost." Actor: council. Action: six-week pilot, named branch, hours, staffing. Success: visits covering staffing cost. Note: naming a missing element is what makes a rating useful, not just 'weak'.

activities.title: Score a clinic claim
activities.instructions:
Original fictional example. A resident writes this claim to the local paper: "The county health office should take action on the long waits at the community clinic, because mornings are crowded and people give up and go home — and any change should stay in place only if the share of morning visitors seen within an hour goes up."

Recall the three-criterion check from the worked example. Who acts: a named decider who could actually decide or fund the change. What exactly to do: a concrete step with details, not just a direction. What counts as success: a stated measure that could show the change worked or failed.

Score this clinic draft. It names a real decider — the county health office — so who acts passes. It also states a measurable standard — the share of morning visitors seen within an hour rising — so what counts as success passes. Exactly one criterion fails, and it fails clearly, so there is a single right pick below.

First, pick the criterion this clinic draft meets least. Then, for the criterion you picked, name the specific missing element in the draft and write one sentence that would supply it.

fields.label: Which criterion does the clinic draft meet least?

choices.label: Who acts — no real decider is named
What exactly to do — no concrete step is given
What counts as success — no measure is stated

fields.rubric_criterion: Identifies the criterion the draft genuinely fails

fields.label: For your picked criterion: the missing element and one sentence that would supply it
criteria: Names the specific missing element in the draft for the criterion picked, quoting or clearly identifying the vague words
Writes one sentence that supplies a concrete actor, action detail, or measurable success standard matching that criterion
Keeps the fix consistent with the supplied facts about the clinic without inventing statistics as evidence

activities.hint: For each criterion, ask what words in the draft supply or fail it: is a real decider named, is "take action" a concrete step with details, and is a success measure stated?
activities.worked_solution:
Which criterion does the clinic draft meet least?

What exactly to do — no concrete step is given

The draft names the county health office, an actual decision-maker over clinic operations, so who acts passes. It also sets a measurable standard — keep the change only if the share of morning visitors seen within an hour rises — so what counts as success passes. What fails is what exactly to do: "take action" names only a direction, with no concrete step such as extra staffing, added hours, or a walk-in window. "What to do" is therefore the uniquely least-met criterion.

For your picked criterion: the missing element and one sentence that would supply it

Model answer: the missing element is any concrete step — the draft says only "take action," with no hours, staffing level, or schedule change specified. A supplying sentence is "The county health office should open an extra walk-in window at the clinic on weekday mornings from opening until noon." A fix that instead changes the actor or the success measure addresses a criterion the draft already passes and would not count, nor would a vague improvement like "handle the waits better."

activities.title: Score your own Sunday draft
activities.instructions:
Original fictional example for practice; here it is your own unaided draft, quoted from your earlier work sample: "Our town should keep the library open on Sundays. Many people work on weekdays. Libraries have books and computers. Last Sunday I saw people waiting outside. Sunday opening would help everyone."

Your task: apply the three-criterion check you just practised — who acts, what exactly to do, what counts as success. Rate this draft on each criterion, and whenever a criterion is not met, name the specific missing element (for example, the exact words the draft relies on instead of a concrete actor, action or measure). A rating like "weak" or "vague" only counts if you say what is missing. If you think part of the draft does some of the work — such as the waiting-outside observation hinting at a success cue — you may treat it that way, as long as you explain how it would need to link to a real measure.

fields.label: Rate your draft on who acts, what exactly to do, and what counts as success, naming each missing element
criteria: Identifies whether a concrete deciding actor is named, or notes the draft only says "our town"
States what a complete action would require (such as pilot details, hours, staffing or duration) or notes that these are absent
Names a measurable success standard, or notes that none is given
Ratings name specific missing words or elements rather than only calling the draft weak or vague
Treats the waiting-outside observation as a partial success cue only by explaining the link to a measure

activities.hint: Go one criterion at a time: ask who could actually decide this, what steps and details the draft commits to, and what result would count as success.
activities.worked_solution:
Rate your draft on who acts, what exactly to do, and what counts as success, naming each missing element

A strong response rates each criterion and names its gap. Actor: the draft says only "our town" — no council or office that could fund and decide Sunday opening is named. Action: "keep the library open on Sundays" gives a direction but no hours, staffing, branch or duration; a pilot with those details would complete it. Success: no measure is stated — "would help everyone" cannot be tested; the waiting-outside observation could serve as a partial cue only if tied to something countable, such as Sunday visit numbers or a comparison with weekday use. Accept reasoned alternatives, including a defensible pass on a criterion, provided the specific missing element is named whenever a rating says the criterion is not met.
